I'm never having children, but something @totenglocke mentioned in another thread made me wonder: are "typical" children nigh impossible to reason with? Is parenting a train of autistic screeching, poo flinging, tantrums, etc? Or are typical children well behaved and mostly rational?

How difficult are "typical" children to raise?

Kids are pretty logical and reasonable. Most children with chronic behavior problems are just showing symptoms of bad parenting and not mental defect.

They are high excitement and their reactions aren't tempered because every situation, interaction and emotion is new. It's a parent's job to demonstrate what do.

There is the occasional young psycho path that will turn out badly no matter what but most children can be easily managed if you understand how they think and are skilled in de-escalation.

Also, one needs practice.

This is very accurate. My son is ridiculously stubborn and strong willed but he's been reasonable since 2ish. Kids are really not that difficult beyond just taking a good amount of effort/time to raise them right.

You have to remember that kids are not blank slates to be designed by parents alone. Genetics and environment play a notable factor in this.

If you have stupid, naturally aggressive children, they will be hard to reason with. If you raise your kids in the ghetto, they are likely to be monsters.

If you are smart, have a decent mate, role-model responsibility in your own life, and raise them in a family-oriented community, you probably will worry more about the occasional sickness and messy room more than youth crime or screaming matches.

Children are an absolute pleasure to be around. They are wonderful. They play quietly. Snuggle often. Give endless hugs and affection. Chat about funny stuff. The science there seems quite junky. For those that didn't read the article, the whole study was little more than asking people essentially 'Do you think an animal torturer turned serial killer is more likely be an atheist or religious believer?' This is little more than a question asking stereotypes of a certain group of people. And that group of people is not atheists, or deists, but serial killers.

For instance, let's create a similar question. A person hacks into a bank and steals a million dollars by transferring a minuscule amount of money from millions of accounts. Is this person more likely to be Asian or black? Everybody is going to say Asian simply because of stereotypes about hackers. Now change the question to robs a convenience mart, and suddenly everybody is going to say black.

The answer to the question is not reflective of views of atheists or religious individuals, but about views of serial killers. This is not a bidirectional association. Serial killers are likely to be atheists is not the same as atheists are likely to be serial killers. Leave it to no less than 13 social scientists (literally - this paper had 13 listed authors) to miss this.
